entries.content_plain:
Introduction
The Philistines set up the ark in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod; whose image is found next morning prostrate before it, broken in pieces, 1Sam 5:1-5 . The Philistines are also smitten with a sore disease, 1Sam 5:6 . The people of Ashdod refuse to let the ark stay with them; and the lords of the Philistines, with whom they consulted, order it to be carried to Gath, 1Sam 5:7 , 1Sam 5:8 . They do so; and God smites the inhabitants of that city, young and old, with the same disease, 1Sam 5:9 . They send the ark to Ekron, and a heavy destruction fags upon that city, and they resolve to send it back to Shiloh, 1Sam 5:10-12 .
Verse 1
Brought it from Eben-ezer unto Ashdod - Ashdod or Azotus was one of the five satrapies or lordships of the Philistines.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> The house of Dagon - On this idol, which was supposed to be partly in a human form, and partly in that of a fish, see the note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.23">Jdg 16:23</reference>. Some think that this idol was the same with Dirceto, Attergatis, the Venus of Askelon, and the Moon. - See Calmet's Dissertation on the gods of the Philistines. <div eID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> The motive which induced the Philistines to set up the ark in the temple of Dagon, may be easily ascertained. It was customary, in all nations, to dedicate the spoils taken from an enemy to their gods: <div eID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9708" type="x-p"/> 1. As a gratitude-offering for the help which they supposed them to have furnished; and, <div eID="gen9708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9709" type="x-p"/> 2. As a proof that their gods, i.e., the gods of the conquerors, were more powerful than those of the conquered. <div eID="gen9709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9710" type="x-p"/> It was, no doubt, to insult the God of Israel, and to insult and terrify his people, that they placed his ark in the temple of Dagon. When the Philistines had conquered Saul, they hung up his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.10">1Sam 31:10</reference>. And when David slew Goliath, he laid up his sword in the tabernacle of the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.8">1Sam 21:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">1Sam 21:9</reference>. We have the remains of this custom in the depositing of colors, standards, etc., taken from an enemy, in our churches; but whether this may be called superstition or a religious act, is hard to say. If the battle were the Lord's, which few battles are, the dedication might be right.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9714" type="x-p"/> Only the stump of Dagon was left - Literally, Only דגן dagon (i.e., the little fish) was left. It has already been remarked that Dagon had the head, arms and hands of a man or woman, and that the rest of the idol was in the form of a fish, to which Horace is supposed to make allusion in the following words: - <div eID="gen9714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> Desinat in piscem mulisr formosa superne "The upper part resembling a beautiful woman; the lower, a fish." <div eID="gen9715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9716" type="x-p"/> All that was human in his form was broken off from what resembled a fish. Here was a proof that the affair was not accidental; and these proofs of God's power and authority prepared the way for his judgments.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> Tread on the threshold - Because the arms, etc., of Dagon were broken off by his fall on the threshold, the threshold became sacred, and neither his priests nor worshippers ever tread on the threshold. Thus it was ordered, in the Divine providence, that, by a religious custom of their own, they should perpetuate their disgrace, the insufficiency of their worship, and the superiority of the God of Israel. <div eID="gen9717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> It is supposed that the idolatrous Israelites, in the time of Zephaniah, had adopted the worship of Dagon: and that in this sense <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.9">1Sam 1:9</reference> is to be understood: In the same day will I punish all those who leap upon the threshold. In order to go into such temples, and not tread on the threshold, the people must step or leap over them; and in this way the above passage may be understood. Indeed, the thresholds of the temples in various places were deemed so sacred that the people were accustomed to fall down and kiss them. When Christianity became corrupted, this adoration of the thresholds of the churches took place.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen9718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9719" type="x-p"/> Smote them with emerods - The word עפלים apholim, from עפל aphal, to be elevated, probably means the disease called the bleeding piles, which appears to have been accompanied with dysentery, bloody flux, and ulcerated anus. <div eID="gen9719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9720" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate says, Et percussit in secretiori parte natium; "And he smote them in the more secret parts of their posteriors." To this the psalmist is supposed to refer, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.66">Psa 78:66</reference>, He smote all his enemies in the Hinder Parts; he put them to a perpetual reproach. Some copies of the Septuagint have εξεζεσεν αυτοις εις τας ναυς, "he inflamed them in their ships:" other copies have εις τας ἑδρας, "in their posteriors." The Syriac is the same. The Arabic enlarges: "He smote them in their posteriors, so that they were affected with a dysenteria." I suppose them to have been affected with enlargements of the haemorrhoidal veins, from which there came frequent discharges of blood. <div eID="gen9720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9721" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint and Vulgate make a very material addition to this verse: Και μεσον της χωρας αυτης ανεφυεσιν μυες· και εγενετο συγχυσις θανατου μεγαλη εν τη πολει; Et ebullierunt villae et agri in medio regionis illius; et nati sunt mures, et facta est confusio mortis magnae in civitate: "And the cities and fields of all that region burst up, and mice were produced, and there was the confusion of a great death in the city." This addition Houbigant contends was originally in the Hebrew text; and this gives us the reason why golden mice were sent, as well as the images of the emerods, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.4">1Sam 6:4</reference>), when the ark was restored.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> The lords of the Philistines - The word סרני sarney, which we translate lords, is rendered by the Chaldee טורני tureney, tyrants. The Syriac is the same. By the Vulgate and Septuagint, satrapae, satraps. Palestine was divided into five satrapies: Ashdod, Ekron, Askelon, Gath, and Gaza. See <reference osisRef="Jos.13.8">Jos 13:8</reference>. But these were all federates and acted under one general government, for which they assembled in council. <div eID="gen9723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9724" type="x-p"/> Let the ark - be carried about - They probably thought that their affliction rose from some natural cause; and therefore they wished the ark to be carried about from place to place, to see what the effects might be. If they found the same evil produced wherever it came, then they must conclude that it was a judgment from the God of Israel.

navigation_sections.title: 1 Samuel 5 · Introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain:
Introduction
The Philistines set up the ark in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod; whose image is found next morning prostrate before it, broken in pieces, 1Sam 5:1-5 . The Philistines are also smitten with a sore disease, 1Sam 5:6 . The people of Ashdod refuse to let the ark stay with them; and the lords of the Philistines, with whom they consulted, order it to be carried to Gath, 1Sam 5:7 , 1Sam 5:8 . They do so; and God smites the inhabitants of that city, young and old, with the same disease, 1Sam 5:9 . They send the ark to Ekron, and a heavy destruction fags upon that city, and they resolve to send it back to Shiloh, 1Sam 5:10-12 .
